cues.text: First, it finds the seven jobs and their permits.
Next, it reads October's books. Excise tax is simply Washington's tax on business sales. The bills to customers, the purchases and the general ledger, the company's main accounting record, all agree.
Now it checks the state's published rules and tax rates online. All fifteen checks are confirmed, and three questions are left for a person.
Then it works out three taxes. B&O, the business and occupation tax, is charged on total sales. Sales tax uses each job site's rate. Use tax covers supplies bought without sales tax.
Eight checks pass; one invoice charged the wrong rate.
Last, it writes the draft return and its workpapers, the math behind every figure.

All done. The draft shows just over $780,000 due for October. Four items stay open. One invoice undercharged sales tax by $284. A customer's reseller permit, which lets it buy without sales tax, is missing. October's books are not yet approved. And a person reviews, signs and files the return by November 25; nothing is filed or paid.
